# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical Reading: Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

Sections 1 to 5 are strong. They use the pilot's own microdata to confirm, with numbers, most of the weaknesses I raised in the Halden paper. The conclusion is the problem. "Entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the authors' own corrected estimate and by the Varden trial, which the comment cites selectively. The novelty argument also holds its preferred explanation to a far lower standard of evidence than it demands of the alternative.

## 1. Arithmetic check

- **Table 2:** 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6% and 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%. All three are correct.
- **Hours:** 34.6/40.3 is a 14.1% fall, and 34.8/40.4 is a 13.9% fall. Both are correct.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014/1.041 − 1 = −2.6%. Correct.
- **Manager versus records:** managers' ratings exceeded the records in 19 of 23 organisations. If over- and under-rating were equally likely, a split this lopsided would happen by chance only about once in 800 tries (one-sided p ≈ 0.0013). The gap is real.

**One inconsistency.** The breakdown of the extra hours does not add up:

| Component | Hours per week |
|---|---|
| Scheduled | 32.0 |
| Longer days (+0.7 hours × 4 days) | +2.8 |
| Logged work on the day off | +1.6 |
| **Implied total** | **≈ 36.4** |
| **Reported actual** | **34.6** |

Either a component is defined differently from how it reads (for example, averaged only over the people who worked the day off), or a figure is wrong. This should be clarified. It doesn't change Table 2, which uses the totals.

## 2. What the comment establishes

- **Attrition was misreported.** This is the most serious new finding. The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". In fact:
  - seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule began;
  - six cited workload or inability to maintain output;
  - only two cited scheduling.

  This is a factual misstatement by the Halden authors, not just a gap in their analysis.
- **Managers overstated output.** The overstatement is systematic but modest: about 4 points.
- **Actual hours fell about 14%, not 20%.** This closely matches Varden's 13% for case-processing work.
- **Revenue fell in real terms.**
- **The sector claim is an artifact.** Because the per-hour metric divides by 0.8, any output index above 80 shows a "gain". I made the same point earlier.

## 3. The abstract claims a correction the analysis doesn't make

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain down to 10.8%. Attrition is the first of those three. But Table 2 corrects only the output measure and the hours. **No adjustment for attrition is made**, and none is attempted. Even a simple bounding exercise would help: for example, assume a plausible output figure for the nine withdrawers and include them in the average. As written, 10.8% is a figure for survivors, presented as if it were a corrected figure.

## 4. The subsets limit what can be concluded

The data note is candid: the 17, 23 and 27 organisations with usable data were not chosen at random, and the estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". But the abstract and conclusion then generalise, first to the whole pilot and then to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. Organisations that use time tracking are probably concentrated in software and professional services, the sectors that did best in the pilot. The direction of any bias is therefore unknown.

Record-based output has weaknesses too:
- "Billable hours delivered" falls almost automatically when hours are cut.
- "Tickets closed" ignores quality.

The 95.1 figure is better than the managers' 98.9, but it is not a clean benchmark.

## 5. "Entirely an artifact" is not supported

**The authors' own best estimate is +10.8%.** "Entirely" requires that remainder to be zero. The only argument offered for that is the novelty section, which is weak (see section 6 below).

**The Varden trial directly contradicts the claim, and the comment leaves this out.** Varden's design has almost every feature this comment recommends:
- randomisation, which removes self-selection;
- administrative output records;
- actual hours from timesheets.

In case-processing work it found output per actual hour up **12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. Even its counter offices showed +6.7%.

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". Yet it does not mention the case-processing result from the same trial. That stratum was larger (7 v 7 offices against 5 v 5) and is at least as reliable. Accepting a trial's negative result while ignoring its positive one is selective use of evidence.

**The two studies actually converge.** Halden's corrected figure (+10.8%) and Varden's randomised figure (+12.5%) are close. Both used actual hours and record-based output. This points to a real per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% in work that is not tied to presence. Two qualifications apply:
- Unlogged hours may shrink it somewhat.
- Varden's exploratory analysis suggests much of the gain may come from cutting meetings.

## 6. The novelty argument applies a double standard

The comment dismisses the meetings hypothesis because it rests on seven offices and an exploratory analysis. But its own novelty argument rests on even less:

- **Two survey points.** The case is an extrapolation from two readings (0.61 SD at month three, 0.29 at month six). A straight line through them actually reaches zero around month nine, not ten. Nothing shows the trend is linear rather than levelling off.
- **The wrong variable.** The data are self-reported energy, not output. The link between energy and productivity is assumed. Ironically, this is the same "fatigue" mechanism I criticised in the Halden paper.
- **Unconvincing setting for Varden.** Varden staff did not choose the change. Nine months in, they still showed the per-hour gain.
- **A rhetorical device.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming [a durable effect]" moves the burden of proof rather than presenting evidence. The honest conclusion is that durability is unknown, not that the effect is zero.

## 7. The critique of the meetings analysis misstates what Varden did

- **What Varden claimed.** Varden said meetings "may account for part" of the gain. It called the analysis exploratory, said it "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up. Varden did not "cite it as a mechanism". The comment is rebutting a stronger claim than the one made.
- **When the data were collected.** "Selected for analysis after the results were known" is inaccurate. Managers asked for the calendar data to be collected in month six of a nine-month trial, before the final results existed.
- **A stronger comparison goes unmentioned.** The comment ignores Varden's randomised comparison of meeting time: 3.8 hours per week in treated offices against 7.1 in control offices. That comparison is far stronger than the r = 0.71 correlation.
- **Meetings are the alternative to novelty.** If the gain comes from removing meetings, it is a structural change and unlikely to fade. Dismissing the meetings explanation while accepting the novelty one is the double standard from section 6.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Revenue benchmark.** Real revenue fell 2.6%, but there is no benchmark against similar firms that did not take part, so this is not evidence of harm either. The authors themselves call revenue a poor proxy. CPI is also only a rough deflator for business revenue.
- **Retail.** The −11.2% figure rests on three organisations.
- **Cost.** Like the papers before it, the comment never addresses cost per unit of output. With full pay and record-based output of about 95, cost per unit rose by about 5% even in the subset of survivors. That is arguably the employer's real question, and it makes a stronger case than "entirely an artifact".

## Bottom line

**Accept:**
- the attrition finding, and that the working paper misdescribed it;
- the manager-overstatement finding;
- the actual-hours correction;
- the real-revenue adjustment;
- the dismantling of the "sector-general" claim.

**Reject:**
- the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. The comment's own figure of about 11% and Varden's randomised +12.5% both contradict it.
- the novelty argument, as presented.
- the dismissal of the meetings explanation, which misstates what Varden claimed.

**Best synthesis of all three documents:**
- In work not tied to presence, there is a per-hour gain of roughly 10–12%, with output per employee down about 2–5%. It is unclear how long the gain lasts, and plausibly much of it comes from cutting meetings rather than from rest.
- In coverage-bound work, output and service fall.
- Cost per unit of output rises in both cases unless the employer hires staff or reorganises the work.
